> **What this case shows** — an angle is not an ordinary number: 0° and 360° are the
> same point, so the ordinary mean and standard deviation give nonsense, and
> directional data need their own statistics. In biomechanics this matters directly —
> the **vector-coding coupling angle** describes how two joints co-vary through a
> movement, and its circular statistics quantify **inter-joint coordination**: the
> mean resultant length **R̄** (0–1) is the coordination *consistency*, and the **mean
> direction** is the dominant coordination *pattern*. On real WBDS walking, the
> knee–ankle coupling angles have mean direction **254°** and **R̄ = 0.195** (weak but
> significantly non-uniform, Rayleigh p = 3×10⁻⁸), and consistency varies across
> subjects (R̄ 0.06–0.29). The ecosystem's `circularSummary` reproduces the canonical
> R **`circular`** package to machine precision: the resultant length matches
> **exactly** (|difference| = 0) and the mean direction to **6×10⁻¹⁴**.

::: {.callout-tip title="The recipe you'll learn"}
**Workflow** — for a sample of angles: call `circularSummary(angles, units)` → read the
**mean direction** and **R̄** (concentration) → test uniformity with `rayleighTest()`.
**Way of thinking** — never average angles arithmetically. The mean *direction* comes
from summing unit vectors; **R̄** (their resultant length) measures how tightly the
angles cluster — R̄ near 1 is tight, near 0 is spread. These are the right descriptors
for coupling angles, phase, and any directional data.
**Ecosystem usage** — `PhysioCore::circularSummary()`, `rayleighTest()` (uniformity),
`watsonWilliamsTest()` (compare mean directions), `circularLinearCorrelation()`.
:::

## Proposition

On real WBDS walking, the knee–ankle coupling angles have mean direction 254° and
R̄ = 0.195 (Rayleigh p = 3×10⁻⁸), and `circularSummary` reproduces the canonical
`circular` package to machine precision (R̄ |diff| = 0, mean direction |diff| = 6×10⁻¹⁴).

## Question & goal

**The question is whether the ecosystem computes directional statistics correctly —
and whether they match the field-standard tool.** Circular statistics are easy to get
wrong (averaging angles arithmetically is a classic bug). The goal is a head-to-head
against the canonical `circular` package on real coupling angles, on the two
definitional quantities — mean direction and resultant length.

## Challenge & approach

Two joints' coupling is summarised by a *coupling angle* per instant; over a movement
these form a sample of angles. We compute their circular statistics with
`circularSummary` and with the `circular` package, and compare — expecting the
definitional quantities (mean direction, R̄) to match exactly.

```
knee, ankle angles → vector-coding coupling angles ┐
                                                   ├─ circularSummary (mean dir, R-bar)
                                                   └─ vs circular::mean.circular / rho.circular
```

## Data

**WBDS — Fukuchi, Fukuchi & Duarte (2018), PeerJ** (figshare 5722711, CC-BY 4.0): five
subjects of treadmill walking. The knee–ankle **vector-coding coupling angles**
(γᵢ = atan2(Δankle, Δknee) mod 360°; Needham et al. 2014) over a gait cycle — 449
angles for WBDS01. Details in
[`artifacts/data_sources.json`](artifacts/data_sources.json).

## Results

![Left: the knee–ankle coupling angles of WBDS01 on the unit circle — each point is one instant's coordination direction; the red arrow is the mean vector (its length is R̄ = 0.195, its angle the mean direction 254°). The cloud is broad (weak concentration) but significantly biased (Rayleigh p = 3×10⁻⁸). Right: the coordination consistency R̄ for all five subjects (0.06–0.29) — a real between-subject spread.](artifacts/figure.png)

*How to read this:* a tight cluster with a long red arrow would mean highly consistent
coordination; here the angles are spread (short arrow, R̄ = 0.20) but not uniform — the
coordination has a preferred direction.

| Quantity | This reproduction | Reference |
|---|---|---|
| Mean direction | **254.32°** | `circular` = 254.32° |
| \|mean direction diff\| | **6×10⁻¹⁴** | 0 |
| Resultant length R̄ | **0.19528** | `circular` = 0.19528 |
| \|R̄ diff\| | **0** | 0 (exact) |
| Rayleigh p | 3.16×10⁻⁸ | 3.66×10⁻⁸ (approx.) |

The definitional statistics match exactly; the Rayleigh p agrees on strong significance
via a slightly different approximation. Values trace to
[`artifacts/circular_summary.csv`](artifacts/circular_summary.csv) and the per-subject
table [`artifacts/circular_by_subject.csv`](artifacts/circular_by_subject.csv).

## Conclusion

The ecosystem's directional statistics are exactly the field-standard `circular`
package's — so its coordination descriptors are numerically trustworthy. The
transferable takeaway: **summarise angles with the mean direction and the resultant
length R̄, never the arithmetic mean; R̄ is coordination consistency, and it is
reproducible to the bit — while significance tests like Rayleigh's are asymptotic
approximations that differ slightly between tools, so lean on the exact statistics.**

## Open questions

- R̄ and the mean coupling direction are the raw material of coordination analysis:
  comparing them between limbs, between groups (the **Watson–Williams test**,
  `watsonWilliamsTest`), or across the gait cycle (phase-binned coupling-angle
  distributions — the standard coordination-variability analysis) would turn these
  validated directional statistics into a coordination study. The between-subject R̄
  spread (0.06–0.29) already hints at individual coordination signatures worth testing.
  *Documented, not escalated.*

## Using this in your own analysis

| Step | Function | Package |
|---|---|---|
| circular summary (mean direction + R̄) | `circularSummary()` | PhysioCore |
| test for a preferred direction | `rayleighTest()` | PhysioCore |
| compare mean directions across groups | `watsonWilliamsTest()` | PhysioCore |
| circular–linear correlation | `circularLinearCorrelation()` | PhysioCore |

**Choosing the parameters.**

- **units** — pass `"degrees"` or `"radians"` to match your data; the functions convert
  internally and report back in the same units.
- **R̄ interpretation** — R̄ ∈ [0, 1]: near 1 = tightly clustered angles (consistent
  coordination); near 0 = dispersed. It is *not* a correlation — it is concentration.
- **significance** — use `rayleighTest()` for a single sample; remember the p-value is
  an asymptotic approximation, so read it as "clearly (non-)significant", not to the
  last digit.

**The recipe, copy-runnable:**

```r
library(PhysioCore)

# angles = a numeric vector of coupling angles (degrees)
cs <- circularSummary(angles, units = "degrees")
cs$mean    # 254.3  -- mean coordination direction
cs$rbar    # 0.195  -- coordination consistency (mean resultant length)
rayleighTest(angles, units = "degrees")$p.value   # 3e-8  -- significantly non-uniform

# exact by construction: matches the canonical `circular` package
# (circular::mean.circular / circular::rho.circular) to machine precision.
```
